samf-senior-1999-r2-02.title: Compare term by term
samf-senior-1999-r2-02.body:
Each term of the numerator is 8 times the corresponding term of the denominator: $2^1=8\cdot2^{-2}$, $2^0=8\cdot2^{-3}$, $2^{-1}=8\cdot2^{-4}$. The ratio is $8$.

**Answer: (B) 8**

samf-senior-1999-r2-03.title: Areas scale with the square
samf-senior-1999-r2-03.body:
The ratio of corresponding sides is $3:\sqrt3=\sqrt3:1$. Areas of similar figures are in the ratio of the squares of the sides: $(\sqrt3)^2:1=3:1$.

**Answer: (C) 3:1**

samf-senior-1999-r2-04.title: Totals
samf-senior-1999-r2-04.body:
The 20 numbers sum to $20\cdot20=400$; the nine sum to $9\cdot9=81$. The other 11 sum to $400-81=319$, with average $319\div11=29$.

**Answer: (C) 29**

samf-senior-1999-r2-05.title: Angle sums
samf-senior-1999-r2-05.body:
In $\triangle BDC$: $\angle DBC+\angle DCB=180^\circ-w$. In $\triangle ABC$: $x+(y+\angle DBC)+(z+\angle DCB)=180^\circ$, so $x=180^\circ-y-z-(180^\circ-w)=w-y-z$.

**Answer: (A) $w-y-z$**

samf-senior-1999-r2-06.title: Express in terms of a common value
samf-senior-1999-r2-06.body:
Let the common value be $k$. Then $a=k+1$, $b=k-2$, $c=k+3$, $d=k-4$. The largest is $c$.

**Answer: (C) $c$**

samf-senior-1999-r2-07.title: Pair up
samf-senior-1999-r2-07.body:
$100^2-99^2=(100+99)(100-99)=199$, $98^2-97^2=195$, ..., $2^2-1^2=3$. This is an arithmetic sequence $199,195,\dots,3$ with 50 terms, whose sum is $\frac{50(199+3)}2=5050$. (Equivalently, each pair equals the sum of its two bases, so the total is $100+99+\cdots+1=5050$.)

**Answer: (A) 5 050**

samf-senior-1999-r2-08.title: Substitute
samf-senior-1999-r2-08.body:
$n=2m-3$, so $m-2n=m-4m+6=6-3m=3(2-m)$, a multiple of 3. It is not always $-3$ or $0$ (e.g. $m=3,n=3$: $m-2n=-3$; $m=4,n=5$: $-6$), nor always odd or always even.

**Answer: (C) a multiple of 3**

samf-senior-1999-r2-10.title: Consecutive integers
samf-senior-1999-r2-10.body:
$m$ and $m+1$ are consecutive, so they have no common factor other than 1, and their product is a power of 2 (a positive integer, so $n\ge0$ and neither factor is 0). Each factor divides $2^n$, so each is $\pm$ a power of 2, and being coprime one of them is $\pm1$. If $m=1$, then $m+1=2$ and $n=1$. If $m+1=1$ then $m=0$ and the product is 0, impossible. If $m=-1$ the product is 0, impossible. If $m+1=-1$ then $m=-2$, product $2$, $n=1$. So the solutions are $(1;1)$ and $(-2;1)$: exactly two.

**Answer: (C) 2**

samf-senior-1999-r2-11.title: Only small factorials matter
samf-senior-1999-r2-11.body:
For $n\ge5$, $n!$ contains the factors 2 and 5, so it ends in 0. The last digit of the sum is that of $1+2+6+24=33$, i.e. 3.

**Answer: (B) 3**

samf-senior-1999-r2-12.title: Sectors
samf-senior-1999-r2-12.body:
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is $108^\circ$. The goat can sweep a sector of radius 10 and angle $360^\circ-108^\circ=252^\circ$. Beyond a neighbouring corner the remaining rope is $10-6=4$ m and it can sweep a sector of radius 4 and angle $72^\circ$ (the exterior angle), on each side. Area $=\pi\cdot10^2\cdot\frac{252}{360}+2\cdot\pi\cdot4^2\cdot\frac{72}{360}=70\pi+\frac{32}5\pi=\frac{382}5\pi\approx240$.

**Answer: (A) 240**

samf-senior-1999-r2-13.title: Count by number of digits
samf-senior-1999-r2-13.body:
Five-digit numbers: all are greater than 5000, and there are $5!=120$. Four-digit numbers: the first digit must be 5, 6 or 7 (3 choices), then $4\cdot3\cdot2$ ways for the other three digits: $3\cdot24=72$. Fewer digits give numbers below 5000. Total $120+72=192$.

**Answer: (D) 192**

samf-senior-1999-r2-14.title: Count for each listed month
samf-senior-1999-r2-14.body:
February (month 2): the odd days, 14 (15 in a leap year). March (3): days not divisible by 3, $31-10=21$. August (8): odd days, 16. December (12): days divisible by neither 2 nor 3 among $1,\dots,31$: $1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,25,29,31$, i.e. 11. June (6): days divisible by neither 2 nor 3 among $1,\dots,30$: $1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,25,29$, i.e. 10. Among the choices June has the fewest, and no other month has fewer (the remaining months have 31, 15, 25, 27, 20, 13, 28 such days).

**Answer: (E) June**

samf-senior-1999-r2-15.title: Heights from $F$
samf-senior-1999-r2-15.body:
$\angle ABF=60^\circ$ so $\angle FBC=30^\circ$, and $\angle FCB=45^\circ$. Drop the perpendicular $FE$ from $F$ to $BC$ with $FE=x$. Then $EC=x$ (45°) and $BE=x\sqrt3$ (30°), so $BC=x(1+\sqrt3)=2$ and $x=\dfrac2{\sqrt3+1}=\sqrt3-1$. The area of $FBC$ is $\frac12\cdot BC\cdot FE=\frac12\cdot2\cdot x=\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt3-1$**

samf-senior-1999-r2-16.title: Who can be telling the truth?
samf-senior-1999-r2-16.body:
If Petra were telling the truth then nobody attended, but then she (who attended) could not be speaking: so Petra lies and at least one learner attended. Everyone who attended tells the truth, and all five answers are different, so at most one learner can be telling the truth. Hence exactly one learner attended, and that learner is the one who said 'one of us attended': Peter. (Check: the other four lie.)

**Answer: (B) 1**

samf-senior-1999-r2-17.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-1999-r2-17.body:
Areas are preserved in ratio under an affine map, so take $ABCD$ to be a unit square with $A=(0,1)$, $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $D=(1,1)$. Then $E=(0,\frac12)$, $F=(\frac12,0)$, $G=(1,\frac12)$, $H=(\frac12,1)$. The line $DE$ is $x-2y+1=0$ and the line $BG$ is $x-2y=0$; these are parallel, at distance $\frac1{\sqrt5}$. Likewise $AF$ and $CH$ are parallel and perpendicular to those, also $\frac1{\sqrt5}$ apart. So $PQRS$ is a square of side $\frac1{\sqrt5}$ with area $\frac15$, and the ratio is $1:\frac15=5:1$.

**Answer: (E) 5:1**

samf-senior-1999-r2-18.title: Set up the lengths
samf-senior-1999-r2-18.body: Label the 8-sided piece $ABCDEFGH$ as in the figure. Then $AB=HG+FE+DC$ (heights add up on the left side) and $AH-BC=FG-ED$ (horizontal runs). The area of the shaded hexagon is $FG\cdot GI-ED\cdot DC$ where $GI=AB-HG$. The longest side among the vertical ones is $AB$, a sum of three distinct numbers, so $AB\ge6$.

samf-senior-1999-r2-18.title: Check the cases for $AB$
samf-senior-1999-r2-18.body:
$AB=8$: $\{HG,FE,DC\}=\{1,2,5\}$ and the other four lengths $\{3,4,6,7\}$ must satisfy $AH+ED=FG+BC$, forcing $AH=7$, $ED=3$, $\{FG,BC\}=\{6,4\}$. The area is largest for $FG=6$, $GI=7$ ($HG=1$), $DC=2$: $6\cdot7-3\cdot2=36$. (The case $\{1,3,4\}$ has no valid assignment of the remaining lengths $\{2,5,6,7\}$.) $AB=7$: $\{1,2,4\}$, $AH=8$, $ED=3$, giving at most $30$. $AB=6$: $\{1,2,3\}$, at most $27$. Hence the maximum is $36$.

**Answer: (E) 36**

samf-senior-1999-r2-19.title: Geometric progression of similar triangles
samf-senior-1999-r2-19.body:
The three circles are the inscribed circles of three similar right-angled triangles, each obtained from the previous one by the same construction (a square is placed in the triangle, cutting off a smaller similar triangle). So each triangle is the previous one scaled by the same factor $k$, and so are the radii of their incircles: the radii are $99,\ 99k,\ 99k^2$. Thus $99k^2=19$ and the middle radius is $r=99k$ with $r^2=99^2k^2=99\cdot19$. Hence $r=\sqrt{19\times99}$.

**Answer: (B) $\sqrt{19\times99}$**

samf-senior-1999-r2-20.title: Fix the upper pairing
samf-senior-1999-r2-20.body:
Number the strings 1 to 6. By symmetry we may suppose the upper ends are tied as $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\{5,6\}$. The lower ends can then be paired in $5\cdot3\cdot1=15$ ways, all equally likely. Count the pairings that give a single ring. String 1 cannot be tied to 2 (that would close a ring of two strings), so its lower end is tied to one of 3, 4, 5, 6: 4 ways; by symmetry take 3. The chain is then $2-1-3-4$. The lower ends of 2, 4, 5, 6 are still free and can be tied in 3 ways: $\{2,4\},\{5,6\}$ (closes the ring $1,2,4,3$ without 5 and 6 - bad); $\{2,5\},\{4,6\}$ (one ring $2-1-3-4-6-5-2$ - good); $\{2,6\},\{4,5\}$ (good). So $4\cdot2=8$ of the 15 pairings give one ring, and the probability is $\frac8{15}$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac8{15}$**
